concepts.name: BM25 and what keyword search is good at
Hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion
Cross-encoder rerankers and what they cost

questions.prompt: BM25 has two main parameters, `k1` and `b` (Elasticsearch's defaults are 1.2 and 0.75). What do they control?

choices.text: `k1` sets how many results to return; `b` sets the minimum score to keep
`k1` sets term-frequency saturation; `b` sets how much document length matters
`k1` weights matches in the title; `b` weights matches in the body
`k1` is the number of query terms; `b` sets the strength of stemming applied to them

questions.explanation: BM25 is a TF-IDF-style score with built-in term-frequency normalisation. `k1` controls the non-linear saturation: the tenth mention of a word adds much less than the first. `b` controls how much a long document's term counts are scaled down, so long pages don't win just by being long. Neither sets a result count or field weights.

questions.prompt: A user searches your support docs for `Error code TS-999`. Why might BM25 find the right page when embedding search doesn't?

choices.text: BM25 understands that TS-999 is an error code and ranks pages about it by meaning
Embedding models strip numbers during tokenization, so `TS-999` is dropped from the query
BM25 is always more accurate than embeddings on short technical queries
BM25 matches `TS-999` exactly; an embedding may only find error-code pages in general

questions.explanation: This is Anthropic's example in its contextual retrieval post: an embedding model may find content about error codes in general but miss the exact `TS-999` match, which lexical search catches. BM25 doesn't understand meaning at all; it scores matching terms. That is why the two are combined: each finds what the other misses.

questions.prompt: Explain BM25 in one paragraph: how it scores a document for a query, and what it can't do.

model_answer.summary: BM25 scores a document by the query terms it contains, weighting rare terms more, giving diminishing credit for repeats and normalising for document length; it matches words, not meaning.
key_points: It adds up a score for each query term that appears in the document
Terms that are rare across the collection count for more than common ones (the IDF part)
More occurrences of a term raise the score with diminishing returns, controlled by `k1`
Scores are normalised for document length, controlled by `b`, so long documents don't win just by size
It only matches the terms themselves (after tokenising), so synonyms and paraphrases score nothing

questions.explanation: BM25 is the default similarity in search engines like Elasticsearch because it is cheap, needs no training and handles exact identifiers well. Its blind spot is meaning, which is the strength of embeddings, and why hybrid search pairs them.

questions.prompt: Is Postgres's built-in `ts_rank` the same as BM25?

choices.text: No: `ts_rank` uses match frequency only, with no global stats like term rarity
Yes: `ts_rank` is simply Postgres's built-in name for BM25 scoring
Yes, once you pass normalisation option 32, which adds IDF weighting
No: `ts_rank` ranks documents by their length only and ignores term matches

questions.explanation: The Postgres docs say `ts_rank` ranks by the frequency of matching lexemes and that the ranking functions don't use any global information. BM25's IDF needs exactly that global information: how many documents contain each term. The normalisation options adjust for document length or scale the score to 0–1, but don't add IDF. Treat `ts_rank` as BM25-like, and say so if asked.

questions.prompt: Which setup lets `WHERE search @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)` use an index on a `chunks` table?

choices.text: A B-tree index on the `body` text column
An HNSW index on the `search` column
A stored generated `tsvector` column, `search`, with a GIN index on it
No index is possible; full-text search always scans every row

questions.explanation: The Postgres docs show adding a column `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', ...)) STORED` and creating a GIN index on it; `@@` then uses the index, and Postgres keeps the column up to date as rows change. A B-tree can't answer `@@` matches, and HNSW is pgvector's index for vectors, not `tsvector`.

questions.prompt: Users type free text into your search box, such as `refund "credit card" -paypal`. Which Postgres function should turn it into a `tsquery`?

choices.text: `to_tsquery`, which expects operators such as `&`, `|` and `!` between the tokens
`websearch_to_tsquery`, which handles quotes, `OR` and `-` without syntax errors
`to_tsvector`, which parses the search text into lexemes for matching
`ts_rank`, which scores the raw text directly as a query

questions.explanation: `websearch_to_tsquery` accepts web-search syntax: quoted text becomes a phrase, `OR` becomes `|`, `-` becomes NOT, and it never raises a syntax error, which matters for raw user input. `to_tsquery` needs its own operator syntax and errors on malformed input, `to_tsvector` builds the document side, and `ts_rank` scores matches.

questions.prompt: Vector search returns `[A, B, C]` and BM25 returns `[C, A, D]` (best first). With reciprocal rank fusion, `score(d) = Σ 1 / (60 + rank)`, ranks starting at 1, what is the fused order?

choices.text: A, B, C, D
C, A, B, D
A, C, B, D
A, C, D, B

questions.explanation: A scores 1/61 + 1/62 ≈ 0.03252 and C scores 1/63 + 1/61 ≈ 0.03227, so A edges out C; both are in both lists, which is what lifts them. B gets only 1/62 ≈ 0.01613 and D only 1/63 ≈ 0.01587, so B beats D by one rank position. Documents missing from a list simply get nothing from it.

questions.prompt: BM25 scores are unbounded, while cosine similarities fall between −1 and 1. Why doesn't RRF need to normalise them before combining?

choices.text: RRF uses only each document's rank in each list, not its raw score
RRF divides every score by the highest score in its list first
BM25 and cosine scores happen to use the same scale in practice
RRF learns a weight for each system from training data

questions.explanation: The RRF paper notes it combines ranks without regard to the arbitrary scores returned by each ranking method, and needs no training examples. Positions are comparable across systems even when scores aren't, which is what makes RRF a simple, robust default for hybrid search.

questions.prompt: Write reciprocal rank fusion in about ten lines of Python (or describe the code precisely), and explain what the constant `k` does and why 60 is the usual value.

model_answer.summary: Loop over each ranked list, add `1 / (k + rank)` to each document's score with ranks starting at 1, then sort documents by total score; `k` softens the gap between top ranks, and 60 comes from the original paper, where it was near-optimal but not critical.
key_points: Keep a dict of scores; for each ranking and each `(rank, doc)` from `enumerate(ranking, start=1)`, add `1 / (k + rank)`
Return the documents sorted by total score, highest first
A document missing from a list gets nothing from that list, so appearing in several lists lifts it
`k` limits how much a first place from one outlier system dominates, while lower ranks still count
k = 60 was fixed in a pilot study by Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher (SIGIR 2009), who found it near-optimal and the choice not critical

questions.explanation: A version: `scores = defaultdict(float)`; `for ranking in rankings: for rank, doc in enumerate(ranking, start=1): scores[doc] += 1 / (k + rank)`; `return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)`. With k = 60, the difference between rank 1 and rank 2 is small, so agreement between systems matters more than any one system's top pick.

questions.prompt: How does a cross-encoder reranker differ from the bi-encoder embedding model you use for retrieval?

choices.text: It produces smaller embeddings that make vector search faster
It embeds the query and each document separately, like a bi-encoder, but with a larger model
It only uses keyword overlap between the query and the document
It reads the query and a document together and outputs one relevance score, with no embedding to store

questions.explanation: The Sentence Transformers docs explain that a cross-encoder passes both texts through the transformer at the same time and outputs a score; it never produces an embedding for one text on its own. That joint reading makes it more accurate than comparing two separately computed embeddings, but nothing can be precomputed for the documents.

questions.prompt: Why do RAG pipelines rerank only the top 100 to 150 candidates instead of running the cross-encoder over the whole corpus?

choices.text: Cross-encoders can only accept 150 documents at a time in one batch
Reranking more than 150 documents makes the final ordering less accurate
Every (query, doc) pair needs its own model pass, so cost grows per candidate
The whole corpus's embeddings would have to be recomputed for every new query

questions.explanation: Because a cross-encoder scores pairs, nothing is computed ahead of time: each query needs one pass per candidate. The Sentence Transformers docs give the scale: clustering 10,000 sentences with a cross-encoder means about 50 million pairs and roughly 65 hours, against about 5 seconds for a bi-encoder. So retrieve cheaply first, then rerank a short list; Anthropic reranked its top 150 down to 20.

questions.prompt: Design a retrieve-then-rerank pipeline for your RAG app. Say what each stage does, what the reranker costs, and how you would decide whether it is worth it.

model_answer.summary: Retrieve a broad candidate set cheaply with hybrid search, rerank it with a cross-encoder, and pass only the top few chunks to the LLM; keep the reranker only if measured retrieval quality improves enough to justify its added cost and latency.
key_points: Stage 1: hybrid retrieval, BM25 plus vector search combined with RRF, returns the top N candidates (for example 100 to 150)
Stage 2: a cross-encoder scores each (query, chunk) pair jointly and reorders them, which is more accurate than embedding similarity
Only the top k (for example 20) reranked chunks go into the prompt
The reranker adds latency and cost that grow with N on every query, so tune N
Measure recall@k or MRR on a golden set with and without reranking; in Anthropic's contextual retrieval tests, failed retrievals fell 49% without reranking and 67% with it

questions.explanation: Each stage trades accuracy for cost in a different place: the first must be cheap over millions of chunks, the second can be expensive because it sees only a hundred or so. Whether reranking pays off depends on your data, which is why the Week's milestone measures every setup rather than assuming.
